title: The Battle Before The Battle
subtitle: Mission Drift
tagline: The work can continue long after the love that once animated it begins to fade.
headline: Mission Drift
headline_sub: When the Organization Forgets Why It Exists
seo_title: Mission Drift: When an Organization Forgets Its Why
seo_description: The church in Ephesus worked hard and still lost its first love. What Revelation 2 teaches leaders about mission drift, motives and returning to why the work began.
og_image_alt: Mission Drift: The work can continue long after the love that once animated it begins to fade. TheWrkShop, Leadership & Culture.

scriptures.text: I know your deeds, your hard work and your perseverance.
Yet I hold this against you: You have forsaken the love you had at first. Consider how far you have fallen! Repent and do the things you did at first.

blocks.text: Jesus commends the church in Ephesus for its hard work, perseverance, and discernment. Yet He confronts it for forsaking its first love, and calls it to remember, repent, and return.
What makes this passage so unsettling is what Jesus commends before He confronts.
This is not an inactive church.
From the outside, they may look exceptionally committed.
Yet Jesus identifies something their activity cannot conceal.
They are doing many things right while something essential has gone wrong.
Consider that.
A church can have a full calendar, committed volunteers, effective programs, and strong doctrinal vigilance.
And still need repentance.
Why?
BECAUSE PRODUCTIVITY AND SPIRITUAL HEALTH ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE.
“IF THE WORK IS STILL SUCCEEDING, OUR HEARTS MUST STILL BE ALIGNED.”
Imagine a ministry that began because someone genuinely cared about people who felt forgotten.
Years later, the ministry has grown.
But now difficult people are viewed as obstacles to efficiency.
The very people the ministry was created to serve have become interruptions.
Nobody intended that outcome.
The organization simply became more attentive to managing the work than remembering why the work mattered.
A man can do the same thing in his marriage: keep every routine and lose the love that started them.
THE MISSION CAN REMAIN ON THE WALL WHILE DISAPPEARING FROM THE HEART.
How does this happen?
Usually gradually.

blocks.caption: Eventually people stop asking whether their hearts are aligned because their schedules are already full.

blocks.text: This is the danger:
WHAT BEGAN AS AN EXPRESSION OF LOVE CAN BECOME A SUBSTITUTE FOR LOVE.
And because the work continues, the drift can stay hidden.
CHRIST EXAMINES MORE THAN WHAT HIS CHURCH ACCOMPLISHES.
He examines its faithfulness to Him.
Jesus does not simply ask the church to feel nostalgic.
He commands a response.
That matters.
Recovering the mission isn’t necessarily returning to yesterday’s methods.
It means returning to the love and obedience that should govern today’s methods.

items: If Jesus examined why we work, not just what we produce, what would He find?
Have people become assignments rather than neighbors?
Does maintaining the organization consume more energy than serving its purpose?
Are we becoming more like Christ as our responsibilities increase?
What would we stop doing if love, not institutional momentum, guided our priorities?

blocks.text: Remember why the work began.
Examine what now drives it.
Confess where fear, ambition, or exhaustion has displaced love.
Then identify one action that makes your original calling visible again.
Not merely in language.
In practice.
The work can continue long after the love that once animated it begins to fade.

Lord Jesus, You see what our reports cannot reveal. Search our motives. Restore what has grown cold. Keep us from pursuing excellence without devotion, productivity without compassion, or influence without obedience. May everything we build remain an expression of love for You and those You entrust to us. Amen.
Productivity and spiritual health are not interchangeable.
The mission can remain on the wall while disappearing from the heart.
What began as an expression of love can become a substitute for love.
Remembering our calling must eventually change how we live.
—TheWrkShop
